parts.title: A week at circus camp
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last August, I spent a week at a circus camp in the mountains. I had always loved watching acrobats on television, but I had never tried anything difficult. My best friend, Lola, said that it was the best week of her life, so I booked a place.

On the first morning, a coach called Dario asked us to choose between juggling, balancing and flying trapeze. I picked the trapeze, although my legs were shaking. First, we practised on a low bar over a thick mat. By Wednesday, I was swinging high above the ground with a rope around my waist.

The hardest thing was not the height. It was learning to trust the person who caught my hands. Dario told us, "Never look down. Look at your partner." It sounds simple, but it took me three days to do it.

On the last night, we gave a show for our families. I was so nervous that I forgot my first move, but my partner just smiled, and we carried on. When the audience clapped, I felt prouder than I had ever felt. I am already saving money for next summer.

questions.explanation: Her best friend said it was the best week of her life, so she booked a place.

questions.explanation: She says she picked the trapeze.

questions.explanation: She says the hardest thing was learning to trust the person who caught her hands.

parts.title: A short history of the circus
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
The modern circus began in London in 1768, when a former soldier called Philip Astley opened a place for horse riding. [1] He chose a circle because it helped the riders to stay on their horses.

Soon, there was a problem. [2] So Astley added other acts to keep people interested. Clowns, rope walkers and jugglers all joined the show, and it became more and more popular.

In the 1800s, circuses started to travel. [3] Large tents could be put up in a day and taken down overnight, so a show could visit a new town every week.

Many of these shows had animals, but attitudes have changed. [4] Today, most famous circuses use only human performers, and some of them have become works of art.

The circus is still popular around the world. [5] Even a small town can enjoy a show, and people of every age still love to watch.
sentences: Some of the first clowns were also famous musicians.
Companies began to use big tents instead of buildings.
The first films were shown in Paris in the 1890s.
Many people now think that it is wrong to keep wild animals in a show.
You do not need a big stadium to enjoy one.
He kept the horses in a field outside the city.
The place was a round ring, not a stage.
Audiences got bored of watching only horses.

gaps.explanation: The first sentence says a place for horse riding; the next one explains why he chose a circle.
Audiences got bored; the next sentence says Astley added other acts to keep people interested.
Circuses started to travel, and the next sentence talks about large tents.
Attitudes have changed, and the next sentence says most circuses now use only people.
The circus is still popular, and "even a small town" follows the idea that no stadium is needed.

parts.title: Street performers
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Street performers work in busy places, [1] as squares and markets. Many of them have a regular job as well, [2] performing does not pay very much. Some perform for only a few hours, but others stay all day. People who walk by can stop [3] watch, and they can give money if they like the show. [4] you want to perform, you need to ask at the town hall for a permit. The best performers often practise [5] hours every day. When the weather is bad, [6] is better to wait indoors.

gaps.explanation: Such as introduces examples: places such as squares and markets.
The second part gives the reason why they have another job.
Stop to watch means stop in order to watch.
The condition: if you want to perform, you need a permit.
For hours says how long they practise.
It is better is a fixed pattern for a general statement.

turns.text: I did. At first I thought the floor was wet, because it had rained all morning, but the stage has a roof.

turns.text: So, Ella, which part of the circus did you like best? Was it the horses?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: The horses were nice, and Dad says I should ride one, but I’m a bit scared. I did try the ladder in the practice tent. I got halfway and came down.

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Hi Mark, it’s Nina. Sorry I didn’t call last night. We left the circus early. It wasn’t because of the rain. It started to come down during the interval, but we have a big umbrella and we’d have stayed. Actually, we nearly left at the start of the second half, because the seats were so hard that my back hurt, but I put my coat under me and it was fine. In the end it was my little brother Tom. He’s only five, he’d been up since six, and he was so tired that his eyes kept closing. He fell asleep on my shoulder, so I carried him to the car. Call me when you can.

question.explanation: The rain did not matter and the hard seats were fixed with a coat; they left because Tom, aged five, was so tired that he fell asleep.

parts.title: A welcome at the circus
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: ringmaster
turns.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the Silver Star Circus. I’m Sacha, the ringmaster, and I’d like to tell you a few things before we begin. The show lasts two hours, with a short break in the middle. Last year it was three hours, but many children were too sleepy at the end, so we made it shorter. In the break you can buy drinks and ice cream at the back, and the toilets are on your left. Now, about our company. We have twenty-five performers this year. Last year there were thirty, but five of them have started a new circus in Spain. Our performers come from eleven different countries. We hoped to have twelve, but one of our dancers couldn’t get her visa in time. So tonight you will hear many languages behind the curtain! In the second half, our clown will choose a volunteer. Please don’t be afraid. He always picks someone from the audience, and never one of the musicians, although they would be happy to help. I promise that nobody will be hurt. Our biggest act is the high wire. The wire is twelve metres above the ground. Last season we used a lower one, only eight metres, but our artists wanted a bigger challenge. There is a safety net, of course. Please stay in your seats during that act and don’t use a flash. Finally, after the show, the performers will wait outside the tent. They will sign programmes if you’d like. They won’t sign posters, because those are too big for the table, and photos are free, so just ask them. Enjoy the show, and thank you for choosing us!

gaps.prompt: The whole evening, with the break, takes ___ hours
gaps.explanation: The show lasts two hours; three hours was last year’s length.

gaps.prompt: The circus employs ___ artists this year
gaps.explanation: There are twenty-five performers this year; thirty is last year’s number.
They come from eleven countries; twelve was only a hope.

gaps.prompt: Volunteers for the clown always come from the ___
gaps.explanation: The clown picks someone from the audience, never a musician.

gaps.prompt: The high wire is ___ metres above the floor
gaps.explanation: The wire is twelve metres above the ground; the eight-metre wire was used last season.

gaps.prompt: After the show the artists will sign their names on ___
gaps.explanation: They will sign programmes, but not posters.

parts.title: An interview with a street performer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Ogden, you’re known for juggling in the street. Why did you start?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Well, it’s a funny story. People think I wanted money, and I did sell a few tickets when I was fourteen, but that wasn’t the reason. I also entered a school competition, and I lost in the first round, so that didn’t help. The truth is I was very shy. I couldn’t talk to people. Juggling gave me something to do with my hands, and slowly I stopped being afraid of people looking at me. My mum says I was a different boy after one summer, and I think she’s right.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Where do you work in the summer?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I used to do schools, and it was nice, but now the best months are all about festivals. Shopping centres asked me last year, though I said no because they’re too noisy and the floor is hard. Festivals have big crowds and a lot of friendly people. I travel to about ten of them, usually with my van full of equipment and a lot of sandwiches.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And in the winter?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Winter is harder. Nobody wants to stand in the cold. I worked in a bakery for one winter, which was OK because I like the smell of bread, but I got up at four, and I couldn’t keep it up. Cleaning shops, never! Now I teach children in the community centre every Saturday, and I’m much happier than I was in that kitchen.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What’s the best part of the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Oh, easy. I do have more free time than my friends, I suppose, and sometimes I meet well-known actors at festivals, which is exciting. But what I really love is when the whole crowd gasps or laughs at the same moment. That tells me I did something right.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Has anything gone wrong in your shows?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Plenty. Last summer the wind was terrible. My hat nearly flew away, but I caught it. The worst bit was that my clubs flew out of my hands and fell into the fountain. I got wet, the crowd loved it, and the show went on, so I didn’t cancel anything.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young person?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Practise in front of your family before you try the street. They will be honest with you, and they are usually kind. Finding a teacher is useful, but you can learn from videos. And saving money is clever, but you can start slowly. Just begin at home, with three balls, and be patient. It took me a whole year to learn a simple pattern.

questions.prompt: Why did Ogden learn to juggle?
questions.explanation: Money and the competition were not the reason; he was shy and juggling made him less afraid of people looking at him.

questions.prompt: Where does he perform in summer?
questions.explanation: Schools are in the past and shopping centres were refused; the best summer work is at festivals with big, friendly crowds.

questions.prompt: How does he earn money in winter?
questions.explanation: He left the bakery because of the early hours and would never clean shops; now he teaches children at the community centre.

questions.prompt: What does he like best about the job?
questions.explanation: Free time and meeting actors are only extras; what he really loves is the whole crowd gasping or laughing together.

questions.prompt: What advice does he give?

questions.explanation: He says to practise in front of family first; a teacher and saving money are useful but not his main advice.
